author: Basil of Caesarea
work: On the Holy Spirit
translation: Blomfield Jackson (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 8), public domain
note: Basil enumerates the titles of the Holy Spirit — 'Spirit of God, Spirit of truth which proceeds from the Father' — as marks of His proper, divine dignity, part of the treatise's case that the Spirit shares the divine nature. DELICACY: the phrase 'which proceeds from the Father' states the Spirit's eternal procession (John 15:26) and must not be read as ontological subordination; in Basil the Spirit is co-equal and co-eternal, ranked WITH not under the Father and Son. Do not quote the procession clause in isolation. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-13).
text: It is called Spirit of God, Spirit of truth which proceeds from the Father, right Spirit, a leading Spirit. Its proper and peculiar title is Holy Spirit; which is a name specially appropriate to everything that is incorporeal, purely immaterial, and indivisible.

author: Basil of Caesarea
work: On the Holy Spirit
translation: Blomfield Jackson (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 8), public domain
note: Basil's baptismal argument for the co-equal ranking of the Spirit: we believe in and are baptized into the one name of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost together — the lex-orandi ground of the Spirit's co-equality with the Father and the Son (cf. Matt. 28:19). A clean pro-Nicene statement placing the Spirit alongside, not below, Father and Son. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-13).
text: For as we believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost, so are we also baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost; first comes the confession, introducing us to salvation, and baptism follows, setting the seal upon our assent.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Gregory's blunt affirmation of the full deity and consubstantiality (homoousios) of the Holy Spirit, against the Pneumatomachi ('Spirit-fighters'). This is Gregory's own statement: his friend Basil, for pastoral reasons, avoided the bare formula that the Spirit is God, and the creed of 381 is more reserved. A clean, non-subordinationist statement. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-13); also matches the 1894 printing (2026-11-18).
text: What then? Is the Spirit God? Most certainly. Well then, is He Consubstantial? Yes, if He is God.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 40 (On Holy Baptism)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7), public domain
note: The celebrated 'One... and the Three' passage — the classic Cappadocian statement of the Trinity as one undivided Godhead in three co-equal persons: to conceive of any One is to be carried to the Whole; the Three together are one undivided Light. A superb, doctrinally safe Trinity quotation (no subordination, no modalism). Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-13).
text: No sooner do I conceive of the One than I am illumined by the Splendour of the Three; no sooner do I distinguish Them than I am carried back to the One. When I think of any One of the Three I think of Him as the Whole, and my eyes are filled, and the greater part of what I am thinking of escapes me. I cannot grasp the greatness of That One so as to attribute a greater greatness to the Rest. When I contemplate the Three together, I see but one torch, and cannot divide or measure out the Undivided Light.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Epistle 101 (To Cledonius the Priest, against Apollinarius)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7), public domain
note: The famous soteriological principle against Apollinarius (who denied Christ a human mind): 'that which He has not assumed He has not healed.' Christ took a complete human nature — body AND rational soul/mind — so that the whole of humanity might be saved. Affirms the FULL humanity of Christ united to His full deity. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-13).
text: If anyone has put his trust in Him as a Man without a human mind, he is really bereft of mind, and quite unworthy of salvation. For that which He has not assumed He has not healed; but that which is united to His Godhead is also saved.

author: Gregory of Nyssa
work: On "Not Three Gods" (to Ablabius)
translation: William Moore & Henry Austin Wilson (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 5), public domain
note: Gregory's signature argument that the single, undivided divine operation (origin in the Father, through the Son, perfected in the Spirit) reveals one Godhead, one power, one nature — so we do not speak of three Gods. DELICACY: 'origin from the Father, proceeds through the Son, perfected in the Holy Spirit' describes the taxis (order) of the ONE divine act, NOT a hierarchy of being; Gregory's whole point is co-equal unity of nature. Quote WITH the surrounding 'the Godhead is one' conclusion, never the taxis clause alone. Excerpt begins mid-sentence at 'every operation' (marked with a leading ellipsis). Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-13).
text: …every operation which extends from God to the Creation, and is named according to our variable conceptions of it, has its origin from the Father, and proceeds through the Son, and is perfected in the Holy Spirit.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 29 (Third Theological Oration, On the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7), public domain
note: Gregory distinguishes the three persons by their eternal relations (unbegotten Father, begotten Son, proceeding Spirit) while insisting the begetting is 'without reference to time' — i.e. co-eternal, not a temporal or creaturely origin. DELICACY: 'Begetter'/'Begotten'/'Emission' name eternal relations of origin, NOT degrees of deity; read in isolation the language could be misheard as subordinationist, but Gregory's timeless-generation qualifier secures co-eternity and consubstantiality (contra Arius/Eunomius). Always quote WITH the 'without reference to time' clause. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-07-13).
text: The Father is the Begetter and the Emitter; without passion of course, and without reference to time, and not in a corporeal manner. The Son is the Begotten, and the Holy Ghost the Emission.

author: Basil of Caesarea
work: On the Holy Spirit
translation: Blomfield Jackson (NPNF 2nd series, vol. 8), public domain
note: Basil's classic defense of the Spirit's coequal deity (§47): we come to know the one God from the one Spirit, through the one Son, to the one Father — and the order runs the other way too. The FULL sentence is quoted deliberately: the reciprocal clause is Basil's own guard against a subordinationist misreading — the order (taxis) runs both directions, which proves co-equality, not a ranking of being. His whole treatise argues the Spirit is glorified WITH, not under, the Father and the Son. Verified verbatim against source_url (apologia-citations, web, 2026-08-24).
text: Thus the way of the knowledge of God lies from One Spirit through the One Son to the One Father, and conversely the natural Goodness and the inherent Holiness and the royal Dignity extend from the Father through the Only-begotten to the Spirit.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 29 (Third Theological Oration, On the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Gregory's classic formula for the incarnation: the Son added a human nature without losing or lessening his deity. Quoted on library/humanity.html, library/nicene-creed.html and library/phil2.html. The excerpt deliberately stops before the section's pre-Chalcedonian union wording ('His inferior Nature, the Humanity, became God'). Verified word for word against the 1894 printing (two archive.org scans), 2026-11-18.
text: He Who is now Man was once the Uncompounded. What He was He continued to be; what He was not He took to Himself.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 29 (Third Theological Oration, On the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: From Gregory's paired litany of the two natures: each human weakness set beside a divine act, one and the same Christ. Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted from the quotation. Verified word for word against the 1894 printing (two archive.org scans) and New Advent, 2026-11-18.
text: He was tempted as Man, but He conquered as God; yea, He bids us be of good cheer, for He has overcome the world. He hungered—but He fed thousands; yea, He is the Bread that giveth life, and That is of heaven. He thirsted—but He cried, If any man thirst, let him come unto Me and drink.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 30 (Fourth Theological Oration, Second Concerning the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Gregory on John 14:28 ('the Father is greater than I'): 'greater' refers to the Father as the unbegotten source from whom the Son is begotten without reference to time (29.2), while equality belongs to the shared divine nature; the quoted passage itself carries the equal-in-nature fence. DELICACY: 'origination' is the eternal begetting, not a beginning in time and not a lower rank of being. In the same section Gregory also grants the other reading, that the Father is greater than the Son 'considered as man', calling it 'true indeed, but … no great thing'. Both readings are orthodox; do not present either as the only one. Verified word for word against the 1894 printing (two archive.org scans), 2026-11-18.
text: For that the same thing should be at once greater than and equal to the same thing is an impossibility; and the evident solution is that the Greater refers to origination, while the Equal belongs to the Nature; and this we acknowledge with much good will.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: One God in three Persons: none more or less God, none before or after, not divided in will or power, the Godhead undivided. The clause 'and all that proceedeth from Him is referred to One' is omitted (marked …) because, compressed, it invites the misreading that the Son as well as the Spirit 'proceeds', and it bears on the Father as sole source, a point at issue in the filioque question; do not use this line for or against the filioque. New Advent modernises this passage, so source_url is the scan of the 1894 printing (vol. 7, p. 322). Verified word for word against the 1894 printing (two archive.org scans), 2026-11-18.
text: To us there is One God, for the Godhead is One, … though we believe in Three Persons. For one is not more and another less God; nor is One before and another after; nor are They divided in will or parted in power; nor can you find here any of the qualities of divisible things; but the Godhead is, to speak concisely, undivided in separate Persons.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Gregory's account of why the Spirit's deity was made plain last: God revealed himself step by step, so the order is providence, not doubt (the reason is in the quoted text). DELICACY: do not quote this as Gregory admitting Scripture is silent on the Spirit's deity; in the same oration he argues it from Scripture and lists the Spirit's scriptural titles and works (31.29-30). Do not use it to support new revelation beyond the apostles, or to settle how Scripture and later church teaching relate; Christian traditions answer that differently. Quoted on library/holy_spirit.html. Verified word for word against the 1894 printing (two archive.org scans), 2026-11-18.
text: The Old Testament proclaimed the Father openly, and the Son more obscurely. The New manifested the Son, and suggested the Deity of the Spirit. Now the Spirit Himself dwells among us, and supplies us with a clearer demonstration of Himself. For it was not safe, when the Godhead of the Father was not yet acknowledged, plainly to proclaim the Son; nor when that of the Son was not yet received to burden us further (if I may use so bold an expression) with the Holy Ghost; …

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 29 (Third Theological Oration, On the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Against those who call the Son 'God' only in a secondary sense, as the Eunomians did and as the 'a god' reading of John 1:1 does today: God in name only is not God. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: What do you mean to say then? That the Son is not properly God, just as a picture of an animal is not properly an animal? And if not properly God, in what sense is He God at all?

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 29 (Third Theological Oration, On the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Gregory's rule for reading the 'lofty' and 'lowly' sayings of Christ: the lofty belong to his deity, the lowly to the one who became incarnate for us. 'Composite condition' is pre-Chalcedonian wording for the incarnate Christ (one person, God and man), not a mixture of natures. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: What is lofty you are to apply to the Godhead, and to that Nature in Him which is superior to sufferings and incorporeal; but all that is lowly to the composite condition of Him who for your sakes made Himself of no reputation and was Incarnate

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 30 (Fourth Theological Oration, Second Concerning the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: On 'he must reign until' (1 Corinthians 15:25): 'until' marks a point without denying what follows; Gregory distinguishes Christ's kingship over all, of which 'there shall be no end' (Luke 1:33), from his work of bringing us into submission, which is completed. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: Until is not always exclusive of that which comes after, but asserts up to that time, without denying what comes after it.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 30 (Fourth Theological Oration, Second Concerning the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: On 'the Son can do nothing of himself' (John 5:19): this 'cannot' is the 'cannot' of God being unable to be evil, not a lack of power. The excerpt deliberately stops before the section's later relation-of-origin wording. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: For as we assert that it is impossible for God to be evil, or not to exist—for this would be indicative of weakness in God rather than of strength—or for the non-existent to exist, or for two and two to make both four and ten, so it is impossible and inconceivable that the Son should do anything that the Father doeth not. For all things that the Father hath are the Son's; and on the other hand, all that belongs to the Son is the Father's.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 30 (Fourth Theological Oration, Second Concerning the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: On 'the only true God' (John 17:3): if 'only' excluded the Son there, 'the only wise God' and 'Who only hath Immortality' would exclude him from wisdom and immortality too. The excerpt stops before the section's argument from Baruch 3:35. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: For if you attribute this only to the Father, where will you place the Very Truth? For if you conceive in this manner of the meaning of To the only wise God, or Who only hath Immortality, Dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto, or of to the king of the Ages, immortal, invisible, and only wise God, then the Son has vanished under sentence of death, or of darkness, or at any rate condemned to be neither wise nor king, nor invisible, nor God at all, which sums up all these points. … I, however, think that the passage That they may know Thee the only true God, was said to overthrow those gods which are falsely so called, for He would not have added and Jesus Christ Whom Thou hast sent, if The Only True God were contrasted with Him, and the sentence did not proceed upon the basis of a common Godhead.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 30 (Fourth Theological Oration, Second Concerning the Son)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: On Mark 13:32 ('nor the Son'): the one who has just described everything up to the hour cannot be ignorant of it as God; the excerpt runs on to Gregory's own conclusion, 'He knows as God, and knows not as Man', with his guard against separating the two. Do NOT pair with 30.16's second answer, which refers the knowledge 'to The Cause'. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: How then can you say that all things before that hour He knows accurately, and all things that are to happen about the time of the end, but of the hour itself He is ignorant? For such a thing would be like a riddle; as if one were to say that he knew accurately all that was in front of the wall, but did not know the wall itself; or that, knowing the end of the day, he did not know the beginning of the night—where knowledge of the one necessarily brings in the other. Thus everyone must see that He knows as God, and knows not as Man;—if one may separate the visible from that which is discerned by thought alone.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Against 'to be from another is to be less': the Son's not being the Father is no more a deficiency than the Father's not being the Son; the excerpt ends on Gregory's own denial, 'not due to either deficiency or subjection of Essence'. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: For indeed it is not some deficiency in the Son which prevents His being Father (for Sonship is not a deficiency), and yet He is not Father. According to this line of argument there must be some deficiency in the Father, in respect of His not being Son. For the Father is not Son, and yet this is not due to either deficiency or subjection of Essence;

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: On 'who ever prayed to the Spirit?': Christian worship and prayer happen in the Spirit, and 'the adoration of One is the adoration of the Three'; Gregory calls this a first answer and defers a fuller one. Do NOT quote the section's later line about the Spirit 'offering prayer or adoration to Himself' on its own. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: for the present it will suffice to say that it is the Spirit in Whom we worship, and in Whom we pray. … the adoration of One is the adoration of the Three, because of the equality of honour and Deity between the Three

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Against the charge of three gods: unlike human beings, whose common nature is a unity 'only conceivable in thought' (31.15), each divine Person is one with the others as with itself, by identity of essence and power. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: But each of these Persons possesses Unity, not less with that which is United to it than with itself, by reason of the identity of Essence and Power.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: On 'the Bible never says it in so many words': drawing out what a text means is not adding to it. Christian traditions differ on how far teaching may rest on what Scripture does not state in so many words (Gregory himself defers to 'the question of the unwritten' at 31.12); do not use this to settle that question. text: But if, when you said twice five or twice seven, I concluded from your words that you meant Ten or Fourteen; or if, when you spoke of a rational and mortal animal, that you meant Man, should you think me to be talking nonsense? Surely not, because I should be merely repeating your own meaning;

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: Part of Gregory's 'swarm of testimonies' from Scripture to the Spirit: the Spirit at every stage of Christ's life. Verified word for word against the hosted 1894 text (fathers/), itself checked against two archive.org scans of the 1894 printing; Bible references inserted by the 1894 editors are omitted. 2026-11-18.
text: Christ is born; the Spirit is His Forerunner. He is baptized; the Spirit bears witness. He is tempted; the Spirit leads Him up. He works miracles; the Spirit accompanies them. He ascends; the Spirit takes His place.

author: Gregory of Nazianzus
work: Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration, On the Holy Spirit)
translation: Charles Gordon Browne & James Edward Swallow (NPNF ser. 2 vol. 7, 1894), public domain
note: After trying the 'an eye, a fountain, a river' and sun-ray-light pictures (31.31–32), Gregory sets them aside: no analogy for the Trinity is adequate.
